The effects of initial substrate concentration, C/N ratio, and temperature
on solid-state anaerobic digestion from composting rice straw
Zhiying Yan a,1, Zilin Song a,1, Dong Li a, Yuexiang Yuan a, Xiaofeng Liu a,⇑, Tao Zheng b
a Key Laboratory of Environmental and Applied Microbiology, Environmental Microbiology Key Laboratory of Sichuan Province, Chengdu Institute of Biology,
Chinese Academy of Science, Chengdu 610041, China
b Nanjing Normal University, Nanjing 210023, China
h i g h l i g h t s
 Solid-state anaerobic digestion from composting rice straw was studied.
 Microbial community was determined by the high-throughput sequencing technique.
 The optimal condition for biogasifcation is 35.6 C, 20% ISC and C/N of 29.6:1.
 Methanogen was shifted from Methanobacterium to Methanoculleus during the process.

a b s t r a c t
This study investigated the possibilities of improving the biogasiﬁcation from solid-state anaerobic diges-
tion (SS-AD) of composting rice straw (RS) based on the optimized digestion temperature, initial sub-
strate concentration (ISC) and C/N ratio. RS compounds, such as lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose,
were signiﬁcantly degraded after composting. A signiﬁcant interactive effect of temperature, ISC and
C/N ratio was found on the biogasiﬁcation of SS-AD of composting RS, and a maximum biogas production
was achieved at 35.6 C, with a 20% ISC and a C/N ratio of 29.6:1. The veriﬁcation experiment conﬁrmed
the optimization results. High-throughput sequencing analysis indicated that microbial communities in
the SS-AD mainly consist of Methanobacteria, Bacteroidia, Clostridia, Betaproteobacteria, and Gammaprote-
obacteria. A dominant Methanobacteria was shifted from Methanobacterium to Methanoculleus during the
SS-AD process. This study provides novel information about the interdependent effects and microbial
behavior of AD.

1. Introduction
As a result of global warming, increased waste disposal and
energy costs and the need for environmentally sustainable waste
management, growing attention has been devoted to the biocon-
version of biomass into methane-rich biogas. This process demon-
strates a wide range of beneﬁcial effects on the environment,
energy and human health, especially in rural areas of developing
countries (Khoramnia et al., 2011). China is one of the largest agri-
cultural countries and produces over 600 million tons of crop straw
residues every year, ranking ﬁrst in the world (MOA, 2011). Among
these sources, rice straw (RS) represents the largest portion and
accounts for 32.3% of the total crop straw output (MOA, 2011).
Although a few traditional methods of RS disposal or utilization
exist, such as providing energy for household cooking and heating,
most of the crops are burned in a ﬁeld, resulting in the emission of
severe environmental pollution, such as greenhouse gases and
nitrogen oxide (Yang et al., 2008). If the RS can be efﬁciently trans-
formed into biogas, then the energy shortage in rural areas of
China, as well as CO2 emission problems, will be alleviated to a cer-
tain extent (Sun et al., 2005).
Anaerobic digestion (AD) has been successfully implemented in
biomass conversion due to its capability of reducing chemical oxy-
gen demand and biological oxygen demand from organic wastes
while providing clean energy (Chen et al., 2008). The AD process
can operate in both liquid and solid states in terms of total solid
(TS) content. In general, the TS content of liquid AD (L-AD) systems
ranges from 0.5% to 15%, whereas solid-state AD (SS-AD) systems
usually operate at TS contents of higher than 15%. Compared with
L-AD, SS-AD has advantages partially due to smaller reactor

capacity requirements, less energy used for heating, and no pro-
cessing energy needed for stirring. The digestate of SS-AD can be
used as fertilizer or pelletized fuel due to the low moisture content,
which is much easier to handle than the efﬂuent remaining after
liquid AD. Additionally, problems related to the ﬂoating and strat-
iﬁcation of ﬁbrous material in L-AD does not occur in SS-AD
(Chanakya et al., 1993), and the biogas production from SS-AD is
comparable to the output of L-AD (Luning et al., 2003). These
advantages resulted in an early development of SS-AD systems at
the industrial scale. However, because of a lack of scientiﬁc knowl-
edge, most digesters based on SS-AD processes are usually depen-
dent on the empirical knowledge of the operators; the AD
performances are not optimized and could therefore be improved.
Several process parameters can be optimized to operate SS-AD: ini-
tial substrate concentration (ISC), carbon/nitrogen (C/N) ratio,
physico-chemical pretreatment of the substrate, type of feedstock,
and temperature (Karthikeyan and Visvanathan, 2012).
A primary parameter that drives SS-AD is the ISC (i.e., water
content). SS-AD industrial plants are operated from 20% to 30%
TS and up to 40% TS for certain technologies (Karthikeyan and
Visvanathan, 2012). Increasing the TS content leads to lower pro-
cess performance in terms of methane production and substrate
conversion
(Abbassi-Guendouz
et
al.,
2012).
Research
by
Fernandez et al. (2008) showed that the methane yield at 30% sol-
ids content was 17% less than that at 20%. Le Hyaric et al. (2012)
observed that TS content affects the various steps of the AD pro-
cess: hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis and methanogenesis.
Digestion temperature is another key factor affecting the per-
formance of SS-AD, both in batch and continuous mode. Several
authors investigated the effect of temperature on the SS-AD pro-
cess and obtained different results. The ﬁndings of Mashad et al.
(2004) indicated that SS-AD under mesophilic conditions exhibited
a poor start-up performance, whereas operating SS-AD systems
under thermophilic conditions (55.8 C) can accelerate the AD pro-
cess. Kim et al. (2002) found a similar phenomenon of higher bio-
gas
yield
during anaerobic digestion of
organic fraction of
municipal solid waste (OFMSW) at thermophilic conditions than
that at mesophilic conditions. However, recent research by Li
et al. (2010) found that total methane production increased with
temperature from ambient to mesophilic conditions, whereas
acidiﬁcation occurred in thermophilic conditions and led to the
inhibition of biogas production. Clearly, the operation temperature
for the SS-AD is currently controversial. From the economical view,
the mesophilic AD is highly promising and will be promoted in the
future because of the lower amount of heat required for the
mesophilic operation.
The C/N ratio is an important indicator for controlling the bio-
logical treatment system of AD. Most studies recommend an oper-
ating C/N ratio range of 20/1 to 30/1 with an optimal ratio of 25/1
for anaerobic bacterial growth in an AD system (Estevez et al.,
2012). Improper C/N ratios can result in high total ammonia
nitrogen (TAN) release and/or high volatile fatty acids (VFA) accu-
mulation in the digester. Both TAN and VFAs are important inter-
mediates and potential inhibitors in the AD process. The optimal
C/N ratio varies with the type of feedstock to be digested. Yen
and Brune (2007) used waste paper to balance the high nitrogen
concentration of algal sludge for methane production and results
showed that the optimized C/N ratio for the co-digestion was
20/1 to 25/1. Romano and Zhang (2008) recommended that the
C/N ratio be maintained at 15/1 for the co-digestion of onion juice
and digested sludge. However, the recent AD work concerning the
C/N ratio was mostly focused on L-AD, and less information is
available about the SS-AD.
The inﬂuence of operating parameters on AD is often studied
separately, and contradictory results found in the literature
maybe attributed to the interdependency (interaction) of these
parameters. To our knowledge, the simultaneous effect of ISC, C/N
ratio and temperature has not yet been investigated on SS-AD per-
formance. However, due to the high sensitivity of dry media, their
interaction may be critical for performing adequate SS-AD, and a
strong interaction among these parameters may be present. The
objective of the present study was to investigate the effects of three
operating parameters, ISC, temperature and C/N ratio, and their
interaction on the performance of SS-AD of RS under batch condi-
tions. A Box–Behnken experimental design (BBD) combined with
response surface methodology (RSM) was applied to determine
the effect of these parameters on the biogasiﬁcation. Microbial com-
munity structures in the SS-AD process were determined using the
Illumina MiSeq platform.
2. Methods
2.1. Substrates and inoculum
Rice straw (RS) was collected from a rice ﬁeld near the city of
Chengdu (Sichuan province, China) and was cut into 30 mm-long
pieces using a grinder. The anaerobic sludge used as inoculum
was collected from an anaerobic digester in a sewage plant in
Chengdu. The substrates and inoculum were individually homoge-
nized and subsequently stored at 4 C until further use. The chem-
ical characteristic the RS and sludge are presented in Table 1.
2.2. Composting pretreatment
Because the components of lignocellulosic biomass (such as lig-
nin, cellulose, and hemicellulose) are so difﬁcult to degrade by bac-
teria-mediated
hydrolysis
that
soluble
compounds
are
less
available for anaerobic microorganisms, the bioconversion efﬁ-
ciency is always limited (Taherzadeh and Karimi, 2008). Thus,
the RS was ﬁrstly composted to facilitate the bioconversion efﬁ-
ciency. The composting method is described as follows: raw RS
was put into a plastic drum, and 0.29 kg of inoculum and 1.57 kg
of water were added into 1 kg of RS to obtain a moisture level of
65%; the mixture was homogenized, and then the drum was cov-
ered with plastic ﬁlm to keep a temperature range of 60–70 C.
After the mixture was allowed to compost for 7 days, the chemical
composition of the RS, including the TS, VS, lignin, cellulose, and
hemicelluloses contents, were determined.
2.3. Solid-state anaerobic digestion (SS-AD)
The SS-AD experiment was performed in two sets. First, based
on the results of the pretreatment experiment, an optimization
experiment was conducted using the BBD method to evaluate the
effect of ISC, temperature and C/N ratio, as well as their interactive
effects, on the biogasiﬁcation of composting RS. The experiment
was conducted in self-designed anaerobic fermentation equip-
ment. The equipment consisted of an anaerobic digester (2.5-L
reagent bottle), a biogas collector (2-L Erlenmeyer ﬂask), and a
1-L Erlenmeyer ﬂask that collect the water discharged from the
collector. The digesters were placed in a constant temperature
incubator to maintain the experimental temperature. The biogas
generated in the digester was transported into the head space of
the bottle using a glass pipe. The water in the bottle was then
pressed out and overﬂowed into the receiver through another glass
pipe. The volume of the discharged water from the bottle repre-
sented the volume of the generated biogas in the digester. Based
on the previous studies, three levels of ISC (20%, 27.5%, 35%), tem-
perature (30 C, 37.5 C, 45 C) and C/N ratio (15:1, 24:1, 34:1)
were designed to evaluate their effect on the biogasiﬁcation. A
550-g sample of composting RS was used as the digestion material,

and the urea was added to adjust the C/N ratio. The amounts of
substrate and urea at different levels are shown in Table 2. The fer-
mentation lasted for 45 days.
BBDs are a class of rotatable or nearly rotatable second-order
designs based on three-level incomplete factorial designs. The
number of experiments (N) required for the development of a
BBD is deﬁned as N = 2k (k  1) + C0, where k is the number of fac-
tors and where C0 denotes the number of central points. Seventeen
continuous-ﬂow experiments were conducted based on the three
levels of the ISC, temperature and C/N ratio. Response surface
methodology (RSM) was used to build the best model and optimize
the fermentation system using Design Expert version 6.06 (Stat
Ease Inc., Minneapolis, MN, USA). The coded levels and correspond-
ing real values of the operating variables considered in the exper-
imental design are summarized in Table 2. Each treatment was
performed in triplicate. One-way ANOVA was employed to study
the primary effect sand interactions between the parameters
selected on biogas production.
In the second experiment, a veriﬁcation experiment was con-
ducted to test the results from the optimization experiment. The
experiment was conducted in a self-designed batch reactor with
a working volume of 34 L. The reactor was 60 cm high and the
radius was 15 cm. The batch reactor was made from organic glass,
the roof, body and baseboard of which was connected with bolts
and sealed with rubber rings. A water pipe and tailpipe was con-
nected with the roof and a drain pipe was connected with the base-
board. Heat tape enwound the body of the reactor to maintain an
appropriate reaction temperature, and a temperature detector
was used to measure the interior-temperature through the hole
of the body. The digestion experiment was operated for 45 days
at the optimal conditions from the optimization experiment.
2.4. Analytical methods
The daily biogas production for each anaerobic digester was
recorded using the water displacement method. The corresponding
cumulative biogas volume was also calculated. The methane con-
tent in the produced biogas was analyzed with Gas Chromatogra-
phy (Model 7890A, Agilent, USA). The TS, VS, and pH of the
materials were determined using the standard water and waste-
water examination methods (APHA, 1998). Total C and total N con-
tent were analyzed using the elemental analyzer (Vario EL Cube,
Elementar Inc., Germany). The cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin
contents were analyzed based on the method described by Van
Soest and Wine (1967). Brieﬂy, this procedure is based on sequen-
tial extraction with neutral and acidic detergents, followed by a
strong acid extraction. The different fractions were as follows: (i)
the soluble fraction extracted by neutral detergent, (ii) hemicellu-
loses extracted by 2 M hydrochloric acid detergent, (iii) cellulose
extracted by 72% sulfuric acid, and (iv) lignin, the difference after
the acid extraction. The micro-area chemical and ﬁber structure
was analyzed through electron microscopy (S300N, Hitachi, Japan)
and Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR) measurements
(Spectrum, Perkin-Elmer, USA).
2.5. High-throughput sequencing-based microbial community analysis
2.5.1. DNA extraction, 16S rRNA gene ampliﬁcation, and sequencing
To analyze the structure of the microbial communities in the
solid-state anaerobic digester, 0.5 g of sludge incubated for 1, 3,
7, 20, 30, and 45 days was used for DNA extraction. Total DNA
was extracted according to the method described previously
(Rademacher et al., 2012). For sequencing, the 16S rRNA genes
were ampliﬁed with primers 515F (50-GTGYCAGCMGCCGCGGTA-
30) and 909R (50-CCCC GYCAATTCMTTTRAGT-30 targeting the bac-
terial and archaeal V4-V5 region in the 16S rRNA gene) with a
10-mer barcode at the 50 end of primer 515F (Tamaki et al.,
2011). To minimize PCR bias, two PCR reactions were set up for
each sample, and the PCR products in the replicate reactions were
pooled. The details for the PCR and related procedures were
described previously (Li et al., 2013). The amplicons from each
sample

sequenced with the Illumina MiSeq platform (Illumina Company,
San Diego, CA, USA).
2.5.2. Sequencing data processing
The raw sequences were sorted based on the unique sample
barcodes, trimmed for sequence quality, and denoised using the
QIIME pipeline (Caporaso et al., 2010). Chimera sequences were
removed using the UCHIME algorithm (Edgar et al., 2011). As the
sequence number varied among samples, we randomly resampled
the sequences to 5600 reads per sample for further analysis. Then,
the sequences were clustered by the complete linkage clustering
method in the QIIME pipeline. Operational taxonomic units (OTUs)
were classiﬁed using 97% identity of the 16S rRNA gene sequence
as a cutoff, and the OTUs table was generated for each sample
and used for statistical analysis. The Shannon diversity index and
Chao1 estimator were calculated at 97% sequence identity in the
Ribosomal
Database
Project
pipeline
(RDP)
(http://pyro.cme.
msu.edu/). The phylogenetic afﬁliation of each sequence was ana-
lyzed with the RDP classiﬁer at a conﬁdence level of 80%. To assure
the accuracy of the RDP classiﬁer results, the representative
sequences of dominant bacteria and archaea were subjected to
BLAST homology search against the non-environmental sequences
and non-metagenomes in the NCBI nucleotide database (http://
blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov).
2.6. Statistical treatment
Data are expressed as the means ± standard deviations of the
triplicate measurements. Differences between mean values were
examined by one-way analysis of variance, and statistical signiﬁ-
cance was assumed at a level of P < 0.05. The statistical analyses
were performed using the software program SPSS 15.0 (SPSS Inc.,
Chicago, USA). The general differences of microbial community
structure were evaluated by principal coordinates analysis (PCoA)
in Fast UniFrac (http://bmf.colorado.Edu/fastunifrac/) using the
relative abundances of the whole microbial communities.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Effect of composting on the chemical composition of RS
Table 3 shows the composition of RS after composting,
expressed in percentage of the initial TS. Compared with untreated
RS, TS content of composting RS were signiﬁcantly decreased by
63.6% (P < 0.05). A considerable amount of lignocellulose appeared
to be decomposed and converted to other components. However,
the decomposition rates were different; the hemicellulose content
decreased by 7.5%, cellulose decreased by 64.5%, and lignin
decreased by 13.6%. More cellulose was decomposed compared
to lignin and hemicellulose. These results indicate that composting
can effectively improve the biodegradability of complex substrates.
Fdez-Guelfo et al. (2011) reported that pretreatment by compost-
ing resulted in a higher speciﬁc microbial growth rate (160–
205%) compared to untreated organic fractions of OFMSW. Thus,
the reason for the decreased lignocellulosic composition of RS may
be due to the higher production of hydrolytic enzymes, which is
induced by the increased speciﬁc microbial growth by composting.
Contrasting with the result from Brummeler and Koster (1990),
who found the pre-composting treatment of OFMSW resulted in
a 19.5% volatile solid loss, our result shows that higher volatile
solid contents were found in composting RS than those of the
untreated sample, indicating that composting produced more
available substances from RS that can be used by methanogen.
Structural modiﬁcations of RS during composting treatment is sup-
ported by microscope observations (Supplementary material 1).
The content of total C did not differ signiﬁcantly between the
untreated straw and the composting straw (P > 0.05), but this does
not imply that composting has no effect on the C fraction of straw
because the C fraction of the total content was only determined in
this study. A portion of the unavailable C fraction may have been
converted to soluble C content that can be used by bacteria. This
hypothesis, however, requires further investigation and laboratory
testing.
3.2. Modeling and optimization of SS-AD performance
3.2.1. 1Modeling of SS-AD for biogas production
Based on the aforementioned analysis, compositing was shown
to exhibit favorable effectiveness on the degradation of the hemi-
cellulose structure of RS; thus, composting is advised as a pretreat-
ment method for SS-AD. BBD and RSM were used in 17 runs of the
experiment to investigate the effect of three variables, ISC, temper-
ature and C/N ratio, on the biogasiﬁcation of SS-AD. The results in
Table 2 were used for ANOVA and multiple regression analysis in
Design-Expert software using the polynomial model equation. This
approach enabled prediction of the optimum degree of biogas pro-
duction
and
its
corresponding
optimum
variables.
One-way
ANOVA was employed to test and analyze different models. The
best-ﬁt model found was a quadratic model for the biogasiﬁcation
of RS. The F-value of the model was 8.40 with a very low probabil-
ity (p) value of 0.00523 (Table 4). This implies a highly signiﬁcant
effect on the biogas production process. However, the ‘‘lack of ﬁt’’
having a p-value of 0.0006 showed signiﬁcance, implying that the
prediction for the ﬁt of the model was not good. Thus, the model
was adjusted to a better prediction as Eq. (1) (built with codiﬁed
factors), where the regression coefﬁcient is high (R2 = 0.92). The
ﬁnal equation used to obtain the highest rate of biogas production
was as follows:

response surface plots that show the simultaneous effect of two

factors on biogas production obtained from Eq. (1). Fig. 1a depicts a
three dimensional plot showing the effects of ISC and temperature
on the biogas production of composting RS. A large change in the
biogas production by changing each parameter indicated that both
parameters and their interaction are effective. The maximum value
was achieved with the low amount of ISC (20%) and moderate tem-
perature (35.6 C). By increasing the ISC, the biogas production
decreased drastically.
Fig. 2b shows that the increasing the temperature and C/N ratio
to the optimal values, as determined by RSM, resulted in increased
biogas production; however, further increases in concentration
resulted in reduced biogas production. The optimal temperature
and C/N ratio was 35.5 C and 29.5. A lower C/N ratio causes
ammonia accumulation and pH values exceeding 8.5, both of
which are toxic to methanogenic bacteria. In contrast, a high C/N
ratio is an indication of rapid consumption of nitrogen by metha-
nogens and results in lower gas production (Verma, 2002). Previ-
ous report shows a wide range of optimal C/N ratios (10–90) in
methane fermentation, but with 30 being the most common in
liquid-digestion (Yen and Brune, 2007), consistent with our results.
The combined effect of ISC and C/N ratio on biogas production is
shown in Fig. 2c. A strong negative interaction between ISC and
C/N was observed when the digestion temperature was ﬁxed at
35 C. The decreased ISC from 35% to 20% resulted in an increase
in biogas production. This phenomena may explained by the bad
performance of mass transfer, which lead the poor performance
of microbial activity (Bufﬁere et al., 2005).
3.3. Results of veriﬁcation experiment of SS-AD
3.3.1. Biogas production and methane content
To determine the validity of the predicted value, the experi-
ments were performed at the optimal conditions. For ease of oper-

yield. The activity of methanogen increased again when organic
acid accumulated to an extent, resulting in the appearance of a
peak in the biogas production. However, the peak value in the bio-

strate is not as high as the initial concentration.

gradually adapting to the AD environment (particularly, the heter-

ideal micro-environment for the growth of the methanogen popu-

3.3.2. Morphological characteristics of RS
The morphological changes that were induced by SS-AD were
examined by SEM and FT-IR spectra to obtain insight into the
structural modiﬁcations of RS during SS-AD (Supplementary mate-
rial 4), the structural loosening of cells with a simultaneous
increase in porosity was found in the digested RS, and partial expo-
sure of cellulose networks, similar to a honeycomb, was found in
the straw after SS-AD was removed. The FT-IR spectra were ana-
lyzed for the RS before and during SS-AD, and the assignments of
the primary recorded bands are shown in Table 5. The digested
RS showed apparent differences with the undigested straw
(Supplementary material 5). The intensities of absorption at 3300–
3600 cm1 and 1600–1650 cm1 were decreased with an increase
of digestion time, indicating that macromolecular organic matter
such as alcohols, phenols, carbohydrates and organic acids, were
degraded gradually. In all of the spectra, aromatic skeletal vibrations
related to the lignin content were assigned at 1509–1515 cm1 and
1100–1200 cm1. The bands in the 1200–890 cm1 region represent
the
polysaccharides,

band
at

represents
b-(1 ? 4) glycosidic linkages. Both of these two bands were related
to the decomposition of cellulose and hemicelluloses. These band
intensities of digested samples were lower than those of undi-
gested samples. The FTIR analysis showed that the changes
included a decrease in the association of lignin with carbohydrates,
and some degradation and solubilization of cellulose and hemicel-
luloses occurred during the process of AD. These structural changes
in the substrate indicated a successful performance of the SS-AD
because the decomposition of these substances means the utiliza-
tion of substrate by the microorganisms in the system.
3.3.3. Microbial community analysis by high-throughput sequencing
To reveal the microbial community structure in the SS-AD,
digestion sludge samples retrieved from the reactor incubated for
1, 3, 7, 20, 30, and 45 days were used to obtain DNA for the ampli-
ﬁcation and subsequent sequencing of a region of archaea and bac-
terial 16S rRNA genes. A total of 129,340 high-quality sequences
were obtained (ranging from 5600 to 10,446 per sample, data
not shown); all of the sequences were aligned and clustered to cal-
culate operational taxonomic units (OTUs) using 97% sequence
identity as a cutoff, resulting in 459–840 OTUs at a sequencing
depth of 3979 reads per sample. Clearly, the Chao1 estimator of
richness, observed species, and Shannon diversity index of the
microbial community at day 3, day 7, and day 20 were higher than
those at day 1, day 30, and day 45, and the highest value was found
at day 20 (Table 6). These results indicated a dynamic change of
microbial communities during the process of SS-AD. The microbial
community seems more complicated in the growing period than
that in the start-up and stabilization period. The differences in
microbial communities between different fermentation stages
were also demonstrated by principal coordinates analysis (PCoA).
This analysis showed a distinct community structure between six
samples (Fig. 2) that can be separated into three groups. The sam-
ples from day 3, day 7, and day 20 were clustered together, the
samples from day 30 and 45 were clustered together, and the sam-
ple from 1th day was clustered alone.
Fig. 3 shows the microbial community composition at class
level in the process of SS-AD. Clearly, the microbial community
changed as the AD proceeded. Methanobacteria, Bacteroidia, Clos-
tridia, Betaproteobacteria, and Gammaproteobacteria are the pri-
mary prokaryotic communities in the SS-AD. Methanobacteria, the
primary community of methanogens belonging to Euryarchaeota
of archaea, increased continuously to the 6.6% in the ﬁrst 7 days,
decreased slightly and then increased throughout the next days.
Methanobacteria composed 1.16% of the community at day 30
and decreased thereafter. This change was consistent with the
dynamics of methane production. A previous study showed that

should cover most methanogens, the highest relative abundance
of Euryarchaeota only accounted for less than 10% of total reads.

oclastic methanogens accounted for 74% of bacteria in an anaerobic
digester of food waste under mesophilic conditions, and they
detected 72% of clones afﬁliated with Methanosaeta and 2% of

than 12%) and abundant Methanosarcina. This discrepancy could
be related to the different microbial reaction for different AD sub-
strate. Additionally, in the present study, the methanogen commu-
nity was overrepresented by the Methanosarcina at the start-up
and growing periods (1–20 days) but decreased gradually as fer-
mentation proceeded, whereas Methanoculleus gradually increased
and was abundant at the stabilization period (20–45 days). The
shifting from Methanosarcina to Methanoculleus during the process
suggested the acetoclastic methanogens, although important in the
initial phase of the reactor start-up and growing period, were dis-
placed by hydrogenotrophic methanogens at the subsequent sta-
bilization period.
4. Conclusion
Composting pretreatment can effectively improve the degrada-
tion of lignocellulosic structure of RS. The optimization experiment
showed a signiﬁcant interactive effect of temperature, ISC and C/N
ratio on SS-AD. The RSM results indicated the optimal conditions of
35.6 C, 20% ISC and a C/N ratio of 29.6:1 for biogasiﬁcation. Met-
hanobacteria, Bacteroidia, Clostridia, Betaproteobacteria, and Gam-
maproteobacteria were the primary microbial communities in SS-
AD of composting RS. The dominant methanogen was shifted from
Methanobacterium to Methanoculleus during the SS-AD process. The
experimental results serve as useful information for understanding
the AD system.
